data.title: Rosacea — viva
data.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Rosacea** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. Define rosacea.**
- Chronic inflammatory disease of central facial skin with flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, papules, pustules and phymatous changes; adults 30–50 y, fair skin (under-recognised in dark skin), women more (men more phymas)

**Q2. Diagnostic phenotypes (ROSCO approach).**
- Diagnostic (1 is enough): persistent centrofacial erythema with periodic intensification; phymatous changes
- Major (2 needed if no diagnostic): flushing/transient erythema, inflammatory papules and pustules, telangiectasia, ocular manifestations (lid margin telangiectasia, blepharitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, scleritis)
- Minor: burning, stinging, oedema, dryness
- Older subtypes (NRS 2002): erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, ocular; variant — granulomatous

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Neurovascular dysregulation (TRPV1/TRPA1 channels — heat, spices, alcohol trigger flushing; PACAP, CGRP)
- Innate immune dysfunction — high kallikrein-5 cleaves cathelicidin into pro-inflammatory LL-37; TLR2 upregulated; mast cells (MMP-9)
- Demodex folliculorum overgrowth and Bacillus oleronius; UV damage, matrix degeneration
- Triggers: sun, heat, hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, exercise, stress, cold wind, topical steroids, cosmetics

**Q4. Clinical features of phymas.**
- Rhinophyma (bulbous nose — men, sebaceous hyperplasia and fibrosis), gnathophyma (chin), metophyma (forehead), otophyma (ears), blepharophyma (eyelids)

**Q5. Ocular rosacea.**
- In up to 50%; may precede skin; meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, chalazia, conjunctival hyperaemia, dry eye, keratitis, corneal ulcers/perforation — refer to ophthalmology; treat with lid hygiene, doxycycline, cyclosporine eye drops

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acne vulgaris (comedones, younger), SLE (malar rash spares nasolabial folds, no pustules, systemic), seborrhoeic dermatitis (scale), perioral dermatitis, steroid-induced rosacea, carcinoid syndrome/mastocytosis (flushing), photosensitivity, Demodex folliculitis, polycythaemia, dermatomyositis, sarcoidosis/lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei (granulomatous)

**Q7. Treatment by phenotype.**
- General: avoid triggers, gentle skin care, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, green-tinted cosmetics
- Persistent erythema: topical brimonidine 0.33% gel or oxymetazoline 1% cream (α-agonist vasoconstrictors — rebound erythema risk)
- Telangiectasia/erythema: PDL 585/595 nm, IPL, KTP laser
- Papules/pustules: topical ivermectin 1% (anti-Demodex — very effective), metronidazole 0.75–1%, azelaic acid 15%, minocycline foam 1.5%; oral doxycycline 40 mg modified-release (sub-antimicrobial) or 100 mg, minocycline; low-dose isotretinoin (0.1–0.3 mg/kg) for refractory
- Flushing: β-blockers (carvedilol, propranolol), clonidine, botulinum toxin, SSRIs (paroxetine)
- Phymas: isotretinoin early; surgical — CO2/Er:YAG laser resurfacing, electrosurgery, decortication
- Ocular: lid hygiene, doxycycline, topical cyclosporine, ophthalmology

**Q8. What is steroid-induced rosacea?**
- Rosacea-like eruption/flare with erythema, telangiectasia, papulopustules and atrophy after prolonged topical steroid use on the face (common in India — fairness creams with steroid); rebound on stopping; treat by stopping steroid (taper), tacrolimus, doxycycline, ivermectin

**Q9. What is the role of Demodex and microbes?**
- Increased density of Demodex folliculorum (>5 mites/cm²) in papulopustular rosacea; mites and their bacterium Bacillus oleronius trigger TLR2-mediated innate inflammation; basis of topical ivermectin 1% (anti-Demodex + anti-inflammatory)

**Q10. What drugs treat persistent erythema and flushing?**
- Topical α-adrenergic agonists — brimonidine 0.33% gel (α2), oxymetazoline 1% cream (α1) — temporary vasoconstriction (rebound erythema possible)
- Vascular lasers/IPL (PDL 585/595 nm, KTP 532 nm) for telangiectasia and erythema; oral β-blockers (carvedilol, propranolol) or clonidine for flushing; botulinum toxin (microinjections)

**Q11. What is the dose of oral doxycycline in rosacea?**
- Doxycycline 40 mg modified-release once daily (sub-antimicrobial anti-inflammatory dose — inhibits MMPs and cathelicidin) or 50–100 mg/day for 8–12 weeks; minocycline 100 mg; azithromycin or metronidazole alternatives; low-dose isotretinoin (0.25 mg/kg or 10 mg/day) for refractory papulopustular and early phyma

**Q12. Rosacea and comorbidities.**
- Associations reported: GI disorders (SIBO, H. pylori, IBD), cardiovascular risk, depression/anxiety, migraine, Parkinson's disease, dementia — evidence variable; triggers to avoid: heat, sunlight, spicy food, hot drinks, alcohol, exercise, stress, cosmetics with alcohol/menthol, topical steroids

## Quick spotter facts
- Central facial erythema + flushing + papulopustules without comedones — rosacea
- Ivermectin 1% cream; brimonidine/oxymetazoline for erythema
- Rhinophyma — men

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Rosacea); ROSCO 2017/2019 phenotype approach. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
